replying_to: Replying to Selective Cross-Domain Consistency Regularization for Time Series Domain Generalization
display_title: Official Review of Paper2657 by Reviewer 49Y5

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper addresses the domain generalization problem in the context of time series classification application. 
They propose to learn representations such that the predicted class distribution is similar across close domains.
They regularize in two settings: fixed and learned selection. 
In the fixed setting, domain closeness is defined through domain's meta-data and human judgment.
In the learned selection setting, closest domain is defined as the nearest neighbor in the logit space. 
Their regularization based algorithm is shown to perform better than ERM and many other DG methods on two publicly available time-series datasets.
content.main_review:
## Strength   
- Sound empirical evaluation strategy on the two datasets considered. 
- Detailed visualization.

## Weakness  
- Important aspects of the algorithm are not well argued. See below. 
- Marginal empirical gains on 1/2 datasets: HHAR.
- Comparisons on only two datasets is limiting. 
- The paper focuses on time-series, but the authors did not argue well why time-series classification is different enough to warrant a separate study. I.e. why does the existing DG methods fail on time-series and why would their method work only on time-series? Unlike time-series, the DG benchmarks in the case of image applications are well-established. Without a good reason for their algorithm's specialization to time-series classification, I will have to assume the worst that the authors are only trying to avoid evaluation on well-studied image/text DG benchmarks. 
- The intuitive explanation for why the method works is unclear to me. In the learned selection setting, the divergence in logits is minimized between a domain and its closest neighbour (closeness captured again by some distance in the logit space). Why minimize logit divergence between two domains that are already close?

The selective regularization aspect is the only novel aspect of the proposed algorithm as far I see. Algorithms that regularize logits or its normalized version are known [1, 2].
However, the authors did not establish convincingly the need for selective regularization through extensive ablation or comparisons with the existing work. 
The following further experiments can provide more evidence:

- Compare with [1] or [2] on the two datasets. 
- Is the difference between 2 and 1 cluster cases of Table 7, i.e. 87.1 and 85.6 significant? What is the p-score?
- Conduct ablation studies where the closest domain is picked randomly in the learned selection setting.
- Demonstrate empirically the negative transfer between the domains and ill-effects of domain invariance across all domains (without selective regularization). 


## Minor  
- I do not understand why the authors pick 80% samples randomly from the target data to make the test set as described in last para of Page 5, why not use them all? 
- Why is proposed (fixed sel) of Table 3 and 2 cluster of Table 7 Avg. numbers differ (87.9 vs 87.1)?

## References
1. Ahmed, F., Bengio, Y., van Seijen, H. and Courville, A., 2020, September. Systematic generalisation with group invariant predictions. In International Conference on Learning Representations.
2. Arpit, D., Xiong, C. and Socher, R., 2019. Predicting with high correlation features. arXiv preprint arXiv:1910.00164.
content.summary_of_the_review:
More work is needed to establish the need for selective regularization. The empirical gains are marginal and the evaluation is limited to two datasets that are not well studied in the literature. 
Also, unclear what is the unique nature of time-series classification over image/text DG.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 49Y5
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and questions. We respond to each concern point-by-point below.

Q1: Motivation of loss term. 

R1: We have included further explanation of our proposed loss term in Section 3.2, highlighted in blue. The motivation of the proposed regularization is to prevent the model from being over-confident in its predictions due to overfitting on spurious features of individual domains, and hence increase robustness to domain shifts. We have included Figure 4 which shows that the model trained with our proposed regularization is better calibrated, and included this motivation to the introduction.

Q2: Focus on time series. 

R2: We focus on time series in this paper because (1) there is a lack of benchmark evaluation on time series, and (2) properties of other data modalities such as image and text may not apply to time series, and vice versa, so it is not necessarily the case that methods that work well on one data modality will work as well on another. As a case in point, the evaluation in (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021) shows that state-of-the-art DG methods achieve similar performance as ERM on image datasets, while our experiments conducted under the same framework find larger differences in the methods' ability to learn and generalize.

Q3: Additional datasets and experiments. 

R3: We have added experiments on more challenging settings for both Bearings and HHAR datasets in Appendix Section B. We selected domains such that target domain conditions are not combinations of source domain conditions. From Table 11 and Table 12, our proposed method outperforms ERM on all target domains in Bearings, and on average in HHAR.

Q4: Additional baselines. 

R4: We have implemented the method Correlation (Arpit et al., 2019) and added results to Table 3 and 4. We did not add (Ahmed et al., 2020) for comparison because its regularization is on the KL divergence of soft labels in two groupings, while we have already shown in Table 6 that regularizing on KL divergence of soft labels between domains is less effective than regularizing on distance of logits in our applications. We have added (Ahmed et al., 2020) as a reference.

Q5: Details on results in Table 7. 

R5: In Table 7, values in the last column (Avg) have standard errors 1.2, 2.8, 2.5 and 3.2. While the values 87.1\% and 85.6\% are not statistically significant, we would like to point out that the standard error is across a limited set of 3 seeds and the training set is slightly different for each seed due to sampling.

Q6: Ablation study in learned selective regularization setting. 

R6: We added an ablation study on the neighbor domain selection and weight function for learned selective regularization in the Appendix Table 13. Selecting the nearest neighbor domain achieves higher accuracy than random selection. While setting the weight as 1 has higher accuracy than RBF kernel in this study, we note that $\xi$ in the RBF kernel is a tunable hyperparameter and the RBF weight approaches 1 as $\xi \rightarrow 0$.

Q7: Empirical demonstration of negative transfer. 
R7: In Table 7, with target domain G, ERM (top row) has accuracy 94.0\% while clustering logits of all domains together (bottom row) has accuracy 92.3\%.

Q8: Clarification of experimental setup. 

R8: We followed the experimental setup in (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021) to pick 80\% target samples as test set across 3 seeds to account for slight variations in test set.

Q9: Clarification of values in Table 3 and 7. 

R9: In Table 3, results are from the full proposed method with both data augmentations and regularization. In Table 7, we subtract data augmentations to study the effect of regularization in isolation.

Q10: Evaluation on image/text DG benchmarks. 

R10: We additionally implemented learned selective regularization on a benchmark image classification dataset TerraIncognita used in (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021), and attained accuracy 48.4\% +/- 0.4, which is comparable to the best reported performance of 48.6\% and better than performance of domain alignment methods (CORAL, MMD, DANN, CDANN) in (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021). However since the focus of this paper is on time series applications, we will leave further exploration on image/text datasets to future work.

(Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021) I. Gulrajani and D. Lopez-Paz. In Search of Lost Domain Generalization. In ICLR, 2021.

(Arpit et al., 2019) D. Arpit, C. Xiong, and R. Socher. Predicting with high correlation features.ArXiv, 2019.

(Ahmed et al., 2020) F. Ahmed, Y. Bengio, H. van Seijen and A. Courville. Systematic generalisation with group invariant predictions. In ICLR, 2020.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 49Y5
content.comment:
Thank you for your additional comments. Due to the limited revision time and the extensive experiments needed for our evaluation setup (leave-one-domain-out evaluation, 3 seeds, tuning with 20 random hyperparameter configurations for each seed), we were unable to add a third dataset. We address your comments below:

Q1: Why existing DG methods fail on time series application.

R1: From our experiments, we observe that existing DG methods do not consistently fail on time series application, but performance is dependent on dataset and source-target combination. In Table 3 and 4, most existing methods outperform baseline ERM on at least one target domain experiment. This behavior is consistent with that observed in image classification, where (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021) showed that the performance of existing methods differs across datasets and can underperform ERM, in fact almost all methods underperformed ERM for DomainNet dataset by varying extents up to 17.5\%. Therefore, the perceived "failure" of existing methods in this paper is not exclusive to time series application. 

Q2: Insignificant gains on the two datasets. 

R2: Our proposed method demonstrates better performance than baseline ERM on both datasets (6.9\% for Bearings and 1\% for HHAR with learned selective regularization).
Compared with the second best method RSC, our proposed method has better performance than RSC (3.5\% with learned selective regularization) for Bearings and comparable performance for HHAR. While our proposed method does not significantly outperform RSC for HHAR, we would like to point out that our proposed method and RSC utilize different strategies for generalization. RSC perturbs the network by zeroing out features during training. Our proposed methods beats domain alignment methods (DANN-DG, CDANN-DG, CORAL-DG, MMD-DG) with significant margins for both datasets, and through this paper, we hope to encourage further considerations of domain relationships to improve domain alignment methods.

Q3: Minimizing logit divergence between domains that are already close.

R3: In Section 3.3.2 for learned selective regularization, the domain $d^{(j)}$ is the nearest neighbor domain to domain $d^{(i)}$ if it is nearest to $d^{(i)}$ for the most number of classes. Firstly, logit divergence between $d^{(i)}$ and $d^{(j)}$ may not be small for all classes, hence our loss term propagates the inter-domain relationships to all classes. Secondly, logit divergence between $d^{(i)}$ and $d^{(j)}$ is small relative to divergences between $d^{(i)}$ and other domains, but may not be small in terms of absolute magnitude, and our loss term aims to minimize the latter. Thirdly, from the ablation study in Appendix Table 3, implementing the loss term between close domains results in better DG performance than implementing it between random domains.

(Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021) I. Gulrajani and D. Lopez-Paz. In Search of Lost Domain Generalization. In ICLR, 2021

content.title: Thanks again for the response
content.comment:
You may have misinterpreted my question on time-series application, what I meant is point 4 under "weakness" in my main review. 

I am looking for clarification on why regularizing representations between already close domains is helpful rather than how it may happen. 

My biggest concern is regarding the limited evaluation, given that the time-series DG datasets are not standardized yet, I expect to see evaluation on a lot more datasets/tasks. 

Unfortunately, your responses did not resolve my concerns, and I am sticking to my original evaluation.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2657 by Reviewer 5iv7

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a regularization to keep consistent predictions across similar domains in time series classification tasks. Different regularizers are used when meta data of domains are available or not. It also introduces data augmentation to enhance robustness. Experiments on two datasets show that the proposed method outperform a series of baselines.
content.main_review:
## Strengths
1. The idea of the paper is clearly presented and easy to follow,
2. Extensive empirical studies are performed, including thorough analysis of the results

## Weakness
1. First of all, the ultimate purpose of this work is to increase generalizability in spite of domain shifts, as the introduction and the experiments indicate. However, the logic between this goal and the proposed consistency regularization is not clearly presented. By making consistent predictions in similar domains, how can it help making accurate predictions in a target domain that is potentially very dissimilar to all the source domains? In other words, the entire work focuses on data transformations ( the domain shift in fact ) that do not twist class relationships too much, as it always assigns zero weight to dissimilar logits. And what if the shift that occurs in the target domain is not that "mild"?
2. The method in case of unavailability of domain meta data is not convincing. The learned selection is dependent on the feature extractor and classifier. It could be an extreme case where dissimilar domains produces close logits initially, and is induced to be closer. The author should explain how to address such a cold-start issue, where reliable weights $w(d^{(i)}, d^{(j)})$ are not available at first.
3.  Essentially the proposed method aligns the soft labels between domains that are evaluated to be similar. Equivalently, it attempts to obtain domain-invariant features using available data in a subset of source domains. In this sense, I don't think the paper provides sufficient novelty in technical aspect. 

## Suggestions
To improve the paper, I think the authors should clearly demonstrate the necessity and feasibility of the proposed consistency regularization for domain generalizability in addition to empirical results.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think the paper needs considerable revisions before it can be published.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2657 by Reviewer 5iv7

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5iv7
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and questions. We respond to each concern point-by-point below.

Q1: Motivation of loss term. 

R1: We have included further explanation of our proposed loss term in Section 3.2, highlighted in blue. The motivation of the proposed regularization is to prevent the model from being over-confident in its predictions due to overfitting on spurious features of individual domains, and hence increase robustness to domain shifts. We have included Figure 4 which shows that the model trained with our proposed regularization is better calibrated, and included this motivation to the introduction.

Q2: Cold-start issue. 

R2: Thank you for raising this issue. We did not observe any serious cold-start issue in our experiments because the task cross-entropy loss typically outweighs the regularization penalty at the beginning of training. On datasets where cold-start issue is suspected, we recommend using a pre-defined schedule to start with a low regularization hyperparameter and increase the value after a number of training iterations.

Q3: Novelty. 

R3: We would like to clarify that our proposed method regularizes the logits of similar domains. The differences from existing work are: (1) we regularize only logits, and not features or soft labels which we show in Table 6 result in worse performance, and (2) our proposed method encourages invariance only on *subsets* of domains and not *all* domains as in existing works, which generalizes the concept of domain-invariance to invariance within domain clusters. The second point allows us to use prior knowledge/meta-data of source domains to improve domain generalization performance.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2657 by Reviewer 9Zbf

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a domain generalization method for time series classification. Their method consists of an additional loss term that equalizes the distribution of logits for each class across select domains. In order to choose domain pairs for consistency regularization, the authors propose either using prior expert knowledge, or estimating it by computing the distance between logits during training. The authors also improve robustness by using simple time-series data augmentations. They benchmark their method against a wide variety of baselines on two time-series datasets, and find that their method outperforms prior work. They then dissect their performance gains in detail through ablation studies.
content.main_review:
## Strengths

The paper is generally well-written and is easy to follow. The authors conduct a robust experimental evaluation against a wide array of baselines, and their method does seem to improve performance. The authors also conduct interesting further analyses to dissect these performance gains.

## Weaknesses

- The authors do not motivate their proposed loss term very well. It is unclear to me why it is desirable to equalize the average class conditional logits across domains, and what types of distributional shifts this would allow the model to be robust to. The authors should provide a simple synthetic example, or mathematical justification, for why this loss term works.

- The authors should try to be more mathematically rigorous in their explanations/justifications. For example, by "label-preserving, but does not preserve class relationships", do the authors mean that $P(Y|X)$ can change across domains, but $P(Y)$ stays the same?

- It seems to me that penalizing the logits in this fashion would lead to poor model calibration. Is this the case?

- There does not seem to be anything in the loss proposed in Section 3.2 that is specific to time-series data. Is there a reason why the authors chose to frame the paper as being specific to time-series, as opposed to evaluating this loss term on other data modalities (e.g. common image-based DG benchmarks)? 

- The time-series augmentations seem very simple and rudimentary relative to other methods which have been used for time-series augmentation in machine learning (e.g. see [1]). 

- In order to improve the difficulty of the experimental evaluation, I would recommend running a set of experiments where all of the domains for a particular user or phone model are left out (for HHAR, and similarly for Bearings). This seems to be a much more realistic use-case, and would be a bigger challenge for domain generalization methods.

- As these two datasets are less known in the domain generalization field, the authors should consider reporting basic dataset statistics like sample sizes and class distributions for each domain in the appendix.

- Both of the datasets that the authors test on are based on high-frequency sensor measurements (long time series with few features). Do the authors believe that their method would work just as well on other time-series datasets with different characteristics, such as clinical data with fewer time steps but many more features (e.g. [2])?

[1] https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0254841

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.00690
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a method for domain generalization which seems to do well experimentally. However, the proposed method is not very well motivated or justified mathematically. I believe that the paper is borderline, pending author responses and fixes.

replying_to: Replying to Selective Cross-Domain Consistency Regularization for Time Series Domain Generalization
display_title: Official Review of Paper2657 by Reviewer aNuK

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors address the problem of domain generalization in time series classification, where the goal is to learn models that are robust to domain shift without access to target domain samples. This is done by assuming that multiple source domains sharing the same label space are available during training. Their approach, selective cross-domain consistency regularization, encourages similar predictions on subsets of source domains that are estimated to be more similar to each other.
content.main_review:
The authors present a relatively simple strategy for cross-domain robustness in time series classification consisting on regularization by domain similarity and data augmentation. The regularization term in (1) though well motivated is somewhat underwhelming due to the fact that i) only accounts for domain-class averages, rather than distribution matching, and ii) that the regularization weights also depend on domain-class averages, which question whether the weights are necessary or whether the hard constrain on both fixed and learned selection (zeroing out some domain combination weights) are responsible for the performance gains and not the weighting itself. That being said, the authors consider both regularizing on features and soft labels and different number of clusters in the ablation study. However, it will be interesting to see the performance of the model without the weighting term.

The results though comprehensive considering that the authors implement a a wide range of baselines not necessarily proposed for time series classification or domain generalization as well as examining the impact of regularization/augmentation, regularization options and number of clusters, seem underwhelming considering that i) the contribution of data augmentation is minimal as shown in Table 5, and ii) the performance of the proposed model is only slightly better than RSC.

Having results on additional datasets will improve the paper considering that in one of the datasets considered the performance gap between the proposed approach and ERM are very close.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper introduces a regularization term for cross-domain consistency that though well motivated is realized heuristically, which questions the generalizability of the proposed approach beyond the datasets considered in the paper, more so considering that in one of the datasets (HHAR) the proposed approach does not perform to differently than the baseline ERM and does not overperform the existing RSC.
